title: The more
hook: always the more, the greater good

segments.voice: Yesterday, cura personalis, care for the whole person. Your line was the whole person. When you asked how someone really was, did you stop and wait for the answer? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

Four letters sit at the top of homework pages in some Jesuit schools, scribbled before the student's name: A, M, D, G. They stand for a Latin motto of the Jesuits, ad maiorem Dei gloriam, for the greater glory of God. Notice the word in the middle. Not for the glory of God. For the greater glory. There's a comparison built into it, a reaching. Jesuits pulled that reaching out into a single Latin word that you'll hear in their schools, retreats and homilies. It's short enough to fit on a wristband. It's easy to get badly wrong. Today's word.
screen: `A. M. D. G.` → `FOR THE GREATER GLORY OF GOD.` → `NOT GREAT. GREATER.`

segments.voice: Magis. Latin for more. It shows up in the Exercises at the very end of the foundation, when Ignatius says we should desire and choose only what leads more to the end for which we are made. More. Not just a good choice; the choice that leads further toward God. Some readers hear that little comparison again and again in the Exercises. Here's the trap. Magis heard carelessly sounds like more hours, more projects, more achievement, more pressure. A Jesuit motto for burnout. That's not what Ignatius means. The more is measured against one thing only: the love and service of God and neighbor. Sometimes the magis is doing more. Sometimes it's doing less, better. Sometimes it's resting, because a tired person loves badly. Sometimes it's saying no to a good thing so there's room for a better one. That's why magis lives right beside yesterday's cura personalis and the indifference from earlier in the Exercises. It's not a whip. It's a question asked with open hands: of the good options in front of me, which one leads more toward love? Jesus describes his own purpose with a kind of more, in the Douay-Rheims of John's Gospel: "I am come that they may have life, and may have it more abundantly." Abundance, not exhaustion. In a plain week, magis might mean making the phone call instead of sending the text. Reading the bedtime story slowly instead of skimming it. Spending the extra five minutes to do a task well. Or closing the laptop, because the more for tonight is sleep.
screen: `MAGIS: MORE.` · `WHAT LEADS MORE TO OUR END.` · `NOT MORE HOURS. MORE LOVE.` · `SOMETIMES THE MORE IS LESS.` · then, large: `LIFE, MORE ABUNDANTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one place to do a little more. Settle, and breathe. Think of something ordinary you'll do in the next day: a meal, a message, a chore, a conversation. Hold two versions side by side: the way you'd usually do it, and a version with a little more love in it. Not more effort for its own sake. More care, more attention, more patience. Then ask honestly whether the more, this time, might be less. If you pray, you can ask God to show you which. The bell holds the time.
Magis. Latin for more: in the Ignatian sense, the choice that leads more toward God and neighbor, which isn't always the busier one. Today's word.
Your line: magis. Today, in one small task, do it with a little more care than it needs, and notice whether that was more or just busier. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Jesuit schools and retreats speak of the magis as choosing what leads more to God's glory and the good of others; some students write AMDG, the Jesuit motto, at the top of their work.
